etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English macche, mecche, from Old English mæċċa, ġemæċċa (“companion, mate, wife, one suited to another”), from Proto-West Germanic *makkjō, *gamakkjō (“partner, equal”), from Proto-Germanic *makô, from Proto-Indo-European *mag- (“to knead, work”). Compare Danish mage (“mate”), Icelandic maki (“spouse”).

definitions.definition: (sports) A competitive sporting event such as a boxing meet (commonly called a "bout"), a baseball game, or a cricket match.

quote.citation: 1886, Lim Hiong Seng, Handbook of the Swatow Vernacular, Singapore: Koh Yew Hean Press:
quote.text: Can you play billiards? / Yes, do you wish to have a match with me? / Let us simply play (a game) for pleasure. We needn't have a match, as I don't like to gamble.

definitions.definition: Any contest or trial of strength or skill, or to determine superiority.

quote.citation: 1605, Michaell Draiton [i.e., Michael Drayton], “The Second Booke of the Barrons Warres”, in Poems: […], London:  […]  [Valentine Simmes] for N[icholas] Ling, →OCLC, stanza 22, page 31:
quote.text: Ferrer his Taberd vvith rich Verry ſpred, / VVell knovvne in many a vvarlike match before;  […]

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “(please specify the page)”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: A solemn match was made; he lost the prize.

definitions.definition: Someone with a measure of an attribute equaling or exceeding the object of comparison.

quote.citation: 1716 February 10 (Gregorian calendar), Joseph Addison, “The Free-holder: No. 12. Monday, January 30. [1716.]”, in The Works of the Right Honourable Joseph Addison, Esq; […], volume IV, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], published 1721, →OCLC:
quote.text: Government  […]  makes an innocent man, though of the lowest rank, a match for the mightiest of his fellow subjects.
Dean Ippolito looks like an ordinary kid.  But at chess, he is a knight of battle.  Most adults are no match for him.

definitions.definition: A candidate for matrimony; one to be gained in marriage.

quote.citation: 1702–1704, Edward [Hyde, 1st] Earl of Clarendon, “(please specify |book=I to XVI)”, in The History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England, Begun in the Year 1641. […], Oxford, Oxfordshire: Printed at the Theater, published 1707, →OCLC:
quote.text: She  […]  was looked upon as the richest match of the West.

quote.citation: 2019 October 23, Pip Dunn, “The next king of Scotland”, in Rail, page 51:
quote.text: The seat to window match is excellent and there are half-size partition screens between bays.

definitions.definition: Equality of conditions in contest or competition.

quote.citation: c. 1602, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Troylus and Cressida”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene v]:
quote.text: It were no match, your nail against his horn.

definitions.definition: A pair of items or entities with mutually suitable characteristics.

quote.citation: c. 1602, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Troylus and Cressida”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene v]:

1648 August 16 (date written; Gregorian calendar), Robert Boyle, Some Motives and Incentives to the Love of God. […] [Seraphick Love], London:  […]  Henry Herringman, […], published 1659, →OCLC, page 6:
quote.text: [I]t hath been obſerv'd, that Love doth ſeldome ſuffer it ſelf to be confin'd by other matches, then thoſe of its ovvne making.

definitions.definition: (metalworking) A perforated board, block of plaster, hardened sand, etc., in which a pattern is partly embedded when a mould is made, for giving shape to the surfaces of separation between the parts of the mould.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English macchen (“to marry; be paired with”), from the noun (see above).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To agree; to be equal; to correspond.

quote.citation: 2021 June 30, Philip Haigh, “Regional trains squeezed as ECML congestion heads north”, in RAIL, number 934, page 52:
quote.text: I'll be interested to see how this service does. It will be basic with fares to match, so will be akin to a budget airline taking on a flag-carrier.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To agree with; to be equal to; to correspond to.

quote.citation: 1913, Mrs. [Marie] Belloc Lowndes, chapter II, in The Lodger, London: Methuen, →OCLC; republished in Novels of Mystery: The Lodger; The Story of Ivy; What Really Happened, New York, N.Y.: Longmans, Green and Co., […], [1933], →OCLC, page 0091:
quote.text: There was a neat hat-and-umbrella stand, and the stranger's weary feet fell soft on a good, serviceable dark-red drugget, which matched in colour the flock-paper on the walls.

quote.citation: 1927, F. E. Penny, chapter 4, in Pulling the Strings:
quote.text: Soon after the arrival of Mrs. Campbell, dinner was announced by Abboye. He came into the drawing room resplendent in his gold-and-white turban.  […]  His cummerbund matched the turban in gold lines.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To equal or exceed in achievement.

She matched him at every turn: she could do as well or better.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make a successful match or pairing.

quote.citation: 2013 June 1, “End of the peer show”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8838, page 71:
quote.text: Finance is seldom romantic. But the idea of peer-to-peer lending comes close. This is an industry that brings together individual savers and lenders on online platforms. Those that want to borrow are matched with those that want to lend.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To unite in marriage, to mate.

quote.citation: 1598–1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “Much Adoe about Nothing”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: […] Adam's sons are my brethren; and truly, I hold it a sin to match in my kindred.

quote.citation: 1712 (date written), [Joseph] Addison, Cato, a Tragedy. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], published 1713, →OCLC, Act I, scene v, page 1:
quote.text: A senator of Rome survived,  Would not have matched his daughter with a king.

definitions.definition: To fit together, or make suitable for fitting together; specifically, to furnish with a tongue and groove at the edges.
(transitive, programming) To be an example of a rule or regex.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English macche, mecche (“wick (of a candle)”), from Old French mesche, meische, from Vulgar Latin micca (compare Catalan metxa, Spanish mecha, Italian miccia), which in turn is probably from Latin myxa (“nozzle, curved part of a lamp”), from Ancient Greek μύξα (múxa, “lamp wick”).

definitions.definition: A device made of wood or paper, at the tip coated with chemicals that ignite with the friction of being dragged (struck) against a rough dry surface.
